e-9438.knowledge_point: Constructing the Line Integral of a Function Over a Circle
e-9438.problem: Find, as a definite integral, an expression for the line integral of the function $f(x,y) = x^2-1,$ traversed once along the circle $C$ with equation $x^2 + y^2 = 1.$
e-9438.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a circle of radius $1$ centered at $O.$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \big\langle \cos{t}, \: \sin{t} \big\rangle, \qquad 0 \le t \lt 2\pi.
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = x^2-1,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}-1 \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡t-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({cos}^{2}⁡t-1)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡t-1\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

e-6305.knowledge_point: Constructing the Line Integral of a Function Over a Part-Circle
e-6305.problem: Find, as a definite integral, an expression for the line integral of the function $f(x,y) = 2x+y^2$ along the quarter-circle $x^2+y^2=4,$ traversed from the point $(0,2)$ to the point $(-2,0)$ in the second quadrant.
e-6305.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a quarter-circle of radius $2$ centered at $O,$ shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057418/assets/d0ae53dd5d0932cbf834a166e851c227f75cb546b591a9fd43930ec06f0e9ddf.png)

The curve $C$ can be parametrized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \big\langle 2\cos{t}, \: 2\sin{t} \big\rangle, \qquad \dfrac{\pi}{2} \le t \le \pi.
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = 2x+y^2,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =4(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(2x+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }4(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

e-9462.knowledge_point: Computing a Line Integral of a Function Over a Circle
e-9462.problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y) =x^2-2$ along the circle $C$ with equation $x^2 + y^2 = 4.$
e-9462.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a circle of radius $2$ centered at $O.$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \big\langle 2\cos{t}, \: 2\sin{t} \big\rangle, \qquad 0 \le t \le 2\pi.
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = x^2-2,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}-2 \\  & =4{cos}^{2}⁡t-2 \\  & =2(2{cos}^{2}⁡t-1) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }2\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=2t,$ $\textrm d u=2\,\textrm d t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\,\text{d}t & =2{\int }_{0}^{4\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡u{|}_{0}^{4\pi } \\  & =2(0-0) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 1
?

Which of the following gives the line integral of the function f(x,y)=xy, traversed once along the circle C with equation (x+1)2+y2=25?

a
25∫02πsin⁡t(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)dt
b
5∫02πsin⁡t(cos⁡t−5)dt
c
25∫02πsin⁡t(cos⁡t−5)dt
d
5∫02πsin⁡t(5cos⁡t−1)dt
e
25∫02πsin⁡t(5cos⁡t−1)dt
Submit

decision.explanation: Parametrize the circle by x=5cos(t)-1 and y=5sin(t), for 0≤t≤2π. The speed is 5, so xy ds=25sin(t)(5cos(t)-1)dt, giving option e. Options b, c, and d also evaluate to the same value, zero, but e directly expresses the scalar line integral using this parametrization.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=xy,$ traversed once along the circle $C$ with equation $(x+1)^{2}+{y}^{2}=25?$
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a circle of radius $5$ centered at $(-1,0).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1,\,5\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25{sin}^{2}⁡t+25{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{25({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1)(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡t(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }5\operatorname{sin}⁡t(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1)\cdot 5\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =25{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 1
?

Which of the following gives the line integral of the function f(x,y)=xy, traversed once along the circle C with equation (x+1)2+y2=25?

a
25∫02πsin⁡t(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)dt
b
5∫02πsin⁡t(cos⁡t−5)dt
c
25∫02πsin⁡t(cos⁡t−5)dt
d
5∫02πsin⁡t(5cos⁡t−1)dt
e
25∫02πsin⁡t(5cos⁡t−1)dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫abf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt.

The curve C is a circle of radius 5 centered at (−1,0). It can be parametrized as

r(t)=⟨5cos⁡t−1,5sin⁡t⟩,0≤t<2π.

Computing r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖, we get the following:

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(5cos⁡t−1)i+ddt(5sin⁡t)j=−5sin⁡ti+5cos⁡tj‖r′(t)‖=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2=(−5sin⁡t)2+(5cos⁡t)2=25sin2⁡t+25cos2⁡t=25(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=5

Now, since f(x,y)=xy, we obtain

f(r(t))=(5cos⁡t−1)(5sin⁡t)=5sin⁡t(5cos⁡t−1).

Therefore, we can write the integral as

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫02πf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt=∫02π5sin⁡t(5cos⁡t−1)⋅5⋅dt=25∫02πsin⁡t(5cos⁡t−1)dt.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing the Line Integral of a Function Over a Circle
content.problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=xy,$ traversed once along the circle $C$ with equation $(x+1)^{2}+{y}^{2}=25?$
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a circle of radius $5$ centered at $(-1,0).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1,\,5\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25{sin}^{2}⁡t+25{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{25({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1)(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =5\operatorname{sin}⁡t(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }5\operatorname{sin}⁡t(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1)\cdot 5\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =25{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t-1)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 2
?

Which of the following gives the line integral of the function f(x,y)=x+y2, traversed once along the circle C with equation x2+y2=4?

a
4∫02π(2cos⁡t+sin2⁡t)dt
b
2∫02π(2cos⁡t+sin2⁡t)dt
c
4∫02π(cos2⁡t+2sin⁡t)dt
d
4∫02π(cos⁡t+2sin2⁡t)dt
e
2∫02π(cos⁡t+2sin2⁡t)dt
Submit

decision.explanation: Use r(t)=(2cos(t),2sin(t)) for 0≤t≤2π. Its speed is 2, and f(r(t))=2cos(t)+4sin²(t). Thus the line integral is 4∫₀²π(cos(t)+2sin²(t))dt, which is option d.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=x+{y}^{2},$ traversed once along the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4?$
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a circle of radius $2$ centered at $O.$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x+{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4{sin}^{2}⁡t)\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 2
?

Which of the following gives the line integral of the function f(x,y)=x+y2, traversed once along the circle C with equation x2+y2=4?

a
4∫02π(2cos⁡t+sin2⁡t)dt
b
2∫02π(2cos⁡t+sin2⁡t)dt
c
4∫02π(cos2⁡t+2sin⁡t)dt
d
4∫02π(cos⁡t+2sin2⁡t)dt
e
2∫02π(cos⁡t+2sin2⁡t)dt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫abf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt.

The curve C is a circle of radius 2 centered at O. It can be parametrized as

r(t)=⟨2cos⁡t,2sin⁡t⟩,0≤t<2π.

Computing r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖, we get the following:

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(2cos⁡t)i+ddt(2sin⁡t)j=−2sin⁡ti+2cos⁡tj‖r′(t)‖=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2=(−2sin⁡t)2+(2cos⁡t)2=4sin2⁡t+4cos2⁡t=4(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=2

Now, since f(x,y)=x+y2, we obtain

f(r(t))=2cos⁡t+(2sin⁡t)2=2cos⁡t+4sin2⁡t.

Therefore, we can write the integral as

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫02πf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt=∫02π(2cos⁡t+4sin2⁡t)⋅2⋅dt=4∫02π(cos⁡t+2sin2⁡t)dt.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms d: r(t)=(2cos(t),2sin(t)) has speed 2, so f(r(t))‖r′(t)‖=4(cos(t)+2sin²(t)). Its integral is 8π; the deliberately submitted option c instead gives 4π.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing the Line Integral of a Function Over a Circle
content.problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=x+{y}^{2},$ traversed once along the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4?$
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a circle of radius $2$ centered at $O.$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x+{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4{sin}^{2}⁡t)\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+2{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 3
?

Which of the following gives the line integral of the function f(x,y)=y3, traversed once along the circle C with equation (x−1)2+(y−1)2=36?

a
6∫02π(6sin⁡t+1)3dt
b
36∫02π(sin⁡t+1)3dt
c
∫02π(6sin⁡t+1)3dt
d
36∫02π(cos⁡t+1)3dt
e
6∫02π(6cos⁡t+1)3dt
Submit

decision.explanation: Parametrize C by r(t)=(1+6cos(t),1+6sin(t)), 0≤t≤2π. Its speed is 6, so the line integral is 6∫₀²π(6sin(t)+1)³dt, option a. Option e is equivalent by a phase shift, but a follows directly from this parametrization.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)={y}^{3},$ traversed once along the circle $C$ with equation $(x-1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=36?$
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a circle of radius $6$ centered at $(1,1).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨6\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1,\,6\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1⟩,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1)j \\  & =-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36{sin}^{2}⁡t+36{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{36({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={y}^{3},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1)^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }((6\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1)^{3})\cdot 6\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1)}^{3}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 3
?

Which of the following gives the line integral of the function f(x,y)=y3, traversed once along the circle C with equation (x−1)2+(y−1)2=36?

a
6∫02π(6sin⁡t+1)3dt
b
36∫02π(sin⁡t+1)3dt
c
∫02π(6sin⁡t+1)3dt
d
36∫02π(cos⁡t+1)3dt
e
6∫02π(6cos⁡t+1)3dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫abf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt.

The curve C is a circle of radius 6 centered at (1,1). It can be parametrized as

r(t)=⟨6cos⁡t+1,6sin⁡t+1⟩,0≤t<2π.

Computing r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖, we get the following:

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(6cos⁡t+1)i+ddt(6sin⁡t+1)j=−6sin⁡ti+6cos⁡tj‖r′(t)‖=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2=(−6sin⁡t)2+(6cos⁡t)2=36sin2⁡t+36cos2⁡t=36(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=6

Now, since f(x,y)=y3, we obtain

f(r(t))=(6sin⁡t+1)3.

Therefore, we can write the integral as

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫02πf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt=∫02π((6sin⁡t+1)3)⋅6⋅dt=6∫02π(6sin⁡t+1)3dt.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing the Line Integral of a Function Over a Circle
content.problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)={y}^{3},$ traversed once along the circle $C$ with equation $(x-1)^{2}+(y-1)^{2}=36?$
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a circle of radius $6$ centered at $(1,1).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨6\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1,\,6\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1⟩,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{cos}⁡t+1)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1)j \\  & =-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36{sin}^{2}⁡t+36{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{36({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={y}^{3},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1)^{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }((6\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1)^{3})\cdot 6\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =6{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t+1)}^{3}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Which of the following gives the line integral of the function f(x,y)=1−y2, traversed once along the circle C with equation (x+3)2+y2=1?

a
2∫02π(1−sin⁡t)2dt
b
2∫02π(cos⁡t−3)2dt
c
∫02π(sin⁡t−3)2dt
d
∫02πcos2⁡tdt
e
∫02πsin2⁡tdt
Submit

decision.explanation: Parametrize C by r(t)=(-3+cos(t),sin(t)), 0≤t≤2π. Its speed is 1, and f(r(t))=1-sin²(t)=cos²(t), giving option d. Option e is equivalent by a phase shift; both integrals equal π.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=1-{y}^{2},$ traversed once along the circle $C$ with equation $(x+3)^{2}+{y}^{2}=1?$
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a circle of radius $1$ centered at $(-3,0).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=1-{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =1-(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({cos}^{2}⁡t)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Constructing the Line Integral of a Function Over a Circle
content.problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=1-{y}^{2},$ traversed once along the circle $C$ with equation $(x+3)^{2}+{y}^{2}=1?$
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a circle of radius $1$ centered at $(-3,0).$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-3)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=1-{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =1-(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =1-{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & ={cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }({cos}^{2}⁡t)\cdot 1\cdot \text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

$$

after.html:
Question 5
?

Which of the following gives the line integral of the function f(x,y)=3−y2, traversed once along the circle C with equation x2+y2=9?

a
3∫02π(1−3cos2⁡t)dt
b
9∫02π(1−3sin2⁡t)dt
c
9∫02πcos2⁡tdt
d
9∫02π(3−sin2⁡t)dt
e
3∫02πcos⁡tdt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫abf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt.

The curve C is a circle of radius 3 centered at O. It can be parametrized as

r(t)=⟨3cos⁡t,3sin⁡t⟩,0≤t<2π.

Computing r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖, we get the following:

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(3cos⁡t)i+ddt(3sin⁡t)j=−3sin⁡ti+3cos⁡tj‖r′(t)‖=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2=(−3sin⁡t)2+(3cos⁡t)2=9sin2⁡t+9cos2⁡t=9(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=3

Now, since f(x,y)=3−y2, we obtain

f(r(t))=3−(3sin⁡t)2=3−9sin2⁡t.

Therefore, we can write the integral as

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫02πf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt=∫02π(3−9sin2⁡t)⋅3⋅dt=9∫02π(1−3sin2⁡t)dt.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing the Line Integral of a Function Over a Circle
content.problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=3-{y}^{2},$ traversed once along the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9?$
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a circle of radius $3$ centered at $O.$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+9{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{9({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=3-{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3-(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =3-9{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(3-9{sin}^{2}⁡t)\cdot 3\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =9{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }(1-3{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫02πf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt=∫02π(3−9sin2⁡t)⋅3⋅dt=9∫02π(1−3sin2⁡t)dt.

before.html:
Question 6
?

Which of the following gives the line integral of the function f(x,y)=ex+y along the quarter-circle x2+y2=25, traversed from the point (−5,0) to the point (0,−5) in the third quadrant?

a
5∫π3π/2e5(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)dt
b
5∫π/2πe5(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)dt
c
25∫3π/22πecos⁡t+sin⁡tdt
d
25∫π3π/2ecos⁡t+sin⁡tdt
e
5∫3π/22πe5(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)dt
Submit

decision.explanation: Parametrize the arc by r(t)=(5cos(t),5sin(t)), with π≤t≤3π/2. This traverses the third quadrant from (-5,0) to (0,-5). The speed is 5 and f(r(t))=e^{5(cos(t)+sin(t))}, giving option a.

after.name: Question 6
after.problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)={e}^{x+y}$ along the quarter-circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=25,$ traversed from the point $(-5,0)$ to the point $(0,-5)$ in the third quadrant?
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $5$ centered at $O,$ shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057418/assets/2ec6f01ab00c17d4888dfefb37c2813139af9c412e99acd1a38680274b0f0ddd.png)

The curve $C$ can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,5\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25{sin}^{2}⁡t+25{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{25({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={e}^{x+y},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & ={e}^{5\operatorname{cos}⁡t+5\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & ={e}^{5(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{e}^{x+y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}{e}^{5(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}\cdot 5\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =5{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}{e}^{5(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

content.problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)={e}^{x+y}$ along the quarter-circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=25,$ traversed from the point $(-5,0)$ to the point $(0,-5)$ in the third quadrant?
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $5$ centered at $O,$ shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057418/assets/2ec6f01ab00c17d4888dfefb37c2813139af9c412e99acd1a38680274b0f0ddd.png)

The curve $C$ can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,5\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+5\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25{sin}^{2}⁡t+25{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{25({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =5\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={e}^{x+y},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & ={e}^{5\operatorname{cos}⁡t+5\operatorname{sin}⁡t} \\  & ={e}^{5(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{e}^{x+y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}{e}^{5(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}\cdot 5\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =5{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}{e}^{5(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 7
?

Which of the following gives the line integral of the function f(x,y)=xe1−y2 along the quarter-circle x2+y2=36, traversed from the point (6,0) to the point (0,6) in the first quadrant?

a
36∫π/2πcos⁡te1−36sin2⁡tdt
b
6∫π/2πcos⁡te1−36sin2⁡tdt
c
36∫0π/2cos⁡te1−sin2⁡tdt
d
6∫0π/2cos⁡te1−6sin2⁡tdt
e
36∫0π/2cos⁡te1−36sin2⁡tdt
Submit

decision.explanation: Use r(t)=(6cos(t),6sin(t)), 0≤t≤π/2, which follows the specified first-quadrant arc. Its speed is 6, and f(r(t))=6cos(t)e^{1-36sin²(t)}. Multiplying by the speed gives option e.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=x\,{e}^{1-{y}^{2}}$ along the quarter-circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=36,$ traversed from the point $(6,0)$ to the point $(0,6)$ in the first quadrant?
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $6$ centered at $O,$ shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057418/assets/c1e3332017b795ed6733a0547e6e449fdba3874f1d1e755118a0687ccaf7448c.png)

The curve $C$ can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨6\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,6\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36{sin}^{2}⁡t+36{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{36({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x\,{e}^{1-{y}^{2}},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{1-(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{1-36{sin}^{2}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{e}^{x+y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{1-36{sin}^{2}⁡t}\cdot 6\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =36{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{1-36{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Which of the following gives the line integral of the function f(x,y)=xe1−y2 along the quarter-circle x2+y2=36, traversed from the point (6,0) to the point (0,6) in the first quadrant?

a
36∫π/2πcos⁡te1−36sin2⁡tdt
b
6∫π/2πcos⁡te1−36sin2⁡tdt
c
36∫0π/2cos⁡te1−sin2⁡tdt
d
6∫0π/2cos⁡te1−6sin2⁡tdt
e
36∫0π/2cos⁡te1−36sin2⁡tdt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫abf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt.

The curve C is a part-circle of radius 6 centered at O, shown below.

The curve C can be parametrized as

r(t)=⟨6cos⁡t,6sin⁡t⟩,0≤t≤π2.

Computing r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖, we get following:

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(6cos⁡t)i+ddt(6sin⁡t)j=−6sin⁡ti+6cos⁡tj‖r′(t)‖=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2=(−6sin⁡t)2+(6cos⁡t)2=36sin2⁡t+36cos2⁡t=36(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=6

Now, since f(x,y)=xe1−y2, we obtain

f(r(t))=6cos⁡te1−(6sin⁡t)2=6cos⁡te1−36sin2⁡t.

Therefore, we can write the integral as

∫Cex+yds=∫0π/2f(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt=∫0π/26cos⁡te1−36sin2⁡t⋅6⋅dt=36∫0π/2cos⁡te1−36sin2⁡tdt.

verification.explanation: The worked computation confirms e. With r(t)=(6cos(t),6sin(t)), 0≤t≤π/2, the speed is 6 and f(r(t))=6cos(t)e^{1-36sin²(t)}. Their product gives the displayed integral in e. The solution's left-hand label e^{x+y} is a typo; its substitution and final expression use the stated function correctly.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing the Line Integral of a Function Over a Part-Circle
content.problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=x\,{e}^{1-{y}^{2}}$ along the quarter-circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=36,$ traversed from the point $(6,0)$ to the point $(0,6)$ in the first quadrant?
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $6$ centered at $O,$ shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057418/assets/c1e3332017b795ed6733a0547e6e449fdba3874f1d1e755118a0687ccaf7448c.png)

The curve $C$ can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨6\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,6\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{36{sin}^{2}⁡t+36{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{36({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =6\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x\,{e}^{1-{y}^{2}},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{1-(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{1-36{sin}^{2}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{e}^{x+y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{1-36{sin}^{2}⁡t}\cdot 6\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =36{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{1-36{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

Which of the following gives the line integral of the function f(x,y)=x+y along a circle of radius 4, traversed from the point (−4,0) to the point (4,0), as shown above?

a
16∫π2π(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)dt
b
4∫π2π(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)dt
c
16∫π2π(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)dt
d
4∫0π(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)dt
e
16∫0π(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)dt
Submit

decision.explanation: The shown lower semicircle is parametrized by r(t)=(4cos(t),4sin(t)), π≤t≤2π. Its speed is 4 and f(r(t))=4(cos(t)+sin(t)), so the line integral is the expression in option a.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057418/assets/761643a777650909b8c7ea5477b4fe246ac4032fe183df5d9ad5cb5e08ac1ecc.png)

Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=x+y$ along a circle of radius $4,$ traversed from the point $(-4,0)$ to the point $(4,0),$ as shown above?
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $4$ centered at $O.$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+16{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{16({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x+y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 4\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =16{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 8
?

Which of the following gives the line integral of the function f(x,y)=x+y along a circle of radius 4, traversed from the point (−4,0) to the point (4,0), as shown above?

a
16∫π2π(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)dt
b
4∫π2π(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)dt
c
16∫π2π(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)dt
d
4∫0π(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)dt
e
16∫0π(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫abf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt.

The curve C is a part-circle of radius 4 centered at O. It can be parametrized as

r(t)=⟨4cos⁡t,4sin⁡t⟩,π≤t≤2π.

Computing r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖, we get the following:

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(4cos⁡t)i+ddt(4sin⁡t)j=−4sin⁡ti+4cos⁡tj‖r′(t)‖=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2=(−4sin⁡t)2+(4cos⁡t)2=16sin2⁡t+16cos2⁡t=16(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=4

Now, since f(x,y)=x+y, we obtain

f(r(t))=4cos⁡t+4sin⁡t.

Therefore, we can write the integral as

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫π2πf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt=∫π2π(4cos⁡t+4sin⁡t)⋅4⋅dt=16∫π2π(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)dt.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing the Line Integral of a Function Over a Part-Circle
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057418/assets/761643a777650909b8c7ea5477b4fe246ac4032fe183df5d9ad5cb5e08ac1ecc.png)

Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=x+y$ along a circle of radius $4,$ traversed from the point $(-4,0)$ to the point $(4,0),$ as shown above?
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $4$ centered at $O.$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+16{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{16({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x+y$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t+4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 4\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =16{\int }_{\pi }^{2\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡t+\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 9
?

Which of the following gives the line integral of the function f(x,y)=x9−y2 along the quarter-circle x2+y2=9, traversed from the point (0,−3) to the point (3,0) in the fourth quadrant?

a
27∫π3π/2cos2⁡tdt
b
27∫3π/22πcos2⁡tdt
c
9∫3π/22πcos2⁡tdt
d
9∫3π/22πsin2⁡tdt
e
27∫π3π/2sin2⁡tdt
Submit

decision.explanation: Use r(t)=(3cos(t),3sin(t)), 3π/2≤t≤2π, with speed 3. On this interval cos(t)≥0, so √(9-y²)=3cos(t). Thus f(r(t))=9cos²(t), giving option b. Options a and e have the same numerical value, 27π/4, but b directly represents the specified arc.

after.name: Question 9
after.problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=x\,\sqrt{9-{y}^{2}}$ along the quarter-circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9,$ traversed from the point $(0,-3)$ to the point $(3,0)$ in the fourth quadrant?
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $3$ centered at $O,$ shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057418/assets/b7c2c6f9e50988629007a06213cb3acf0a48f9951f026fb70d5a986b760abdfe.png)

The curve $C$ can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{3\pi }{2}\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+9{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{9({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x\,\sqrt{9-{y}^{2}},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\sqrt{9-(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\sqrt{9-9{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =9{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\,\sqrt{9-{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }9{cos}^{2}⁡t\cdot 3\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =27{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

Which of the following gives the line integral of the function f(x,y)=x9−y2 along the quarter-circle x2+y2=9, traversed from the point (0,−3) to the point (3,0) in the fourth quadrant?

a
27∫π3π/2cos2⁡tdt
b
27∫3π/22πcos2⁡tdt
c
9∫3π/22πcos2⁡tdt
d
9∫3π/22πsin2⁡tdt
e
27∫π3π/2sin2⁡tdt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫abf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt.

The curve C is a part-circle of radius 3 centered at O, shown below.

The curve C can be parametrized as

r(t)=⟨3cos⁡t,3sin⁡t⟩,3π2≤t≤2π.

Computing r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖, we get following:

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(3cos⁡t)i+ddt(3sin⁡t)j=−3sin⁡ti+3cos⁡tj‖r′(t)‖=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2=(−3sin⁡t)2+(3cos⁡t)2=9sin2⁡t+9cos2⁡t=9(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=3

Now, since f(x,y)=x9−y2, we obtain

f(r(t))=3cos⁡t9−(3sin⁡t)2=3cos⁡t9−9sin2⁡t=3cos⁡t9cos2⁡t=9cos2⁡t.

Therefore, we can write the integral as

∫Cx9−y2ds=∫3π/22πf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt=∫3π/22π9cos2⁡t⋅3⋅dt=27∫3π/22πcos2⁡tdt.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms b. For r(t)=(3cos(t),3sin(t)), 3π/2≤t≤2π, the speed is 3 and cos(t)≥0. Hence √(9-y²)=3cos(t), giving 27cos²(t)dt. Options a and e also evaluate to 27π/4, despite the displayed rejection of e; b directly matches the specified arc and worked solution.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing the Line Integral of a Function Over a Part-Circle
content.problem: Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=x\,\sqrt{9-{y}^{2}}$ along the quarter-circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9,$ traversed from the point $(0,-3)$ to the point $(3,0)$ in the fourth quadrant?
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $3$ centered at $O,$ shown below. 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057418/assets/b7c2c6f9e50988629007a06213cb3acf0a48f9951f026fb70d5a986b760abdfe.png)

The curve $C$ can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{3\pi }{2}\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+9{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{9({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x\,\sqrt{9-{y}^{2}},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\sqrt{9-(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\sqrt{9-9{sin}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =9{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\,\sqrt{9-{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }9{cos}^{2}⁡t\cdot 3\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =27{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }{cos}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10

Which of the following gives the line integral of the function f(x,y)=9−x2 along a circle of radius 3, traversed from the point (3,0) to the point (0,3), as shown above?

a
9∫0π/2cos2⁡tdt
b
27∫π/2πcos2⁡tdt
c
9∫0π/2sin2⁡tdt
d
27∫π/2πsin2⁡tdt
e
27∫0π/2sin2⁡tdt
Submit

decision.explanation: Parametrize the shown arc by r(t)=(3cos(t),3sin(t)), 0≤t≤π/2. Its speed is 3, and 9-x²=9sin²(t), giving option e. Options b and d also equal 27π/4, but e directly represents the specified arc.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057418/assets/4403bd230338dee226429d3f8f3ac8eaede1152aff0b6b18bd2e7ad9f3a3b8e3.png)

Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=9-{x}^{2}$ along a circle of radius $3,$ traversed from the point $(3,0)$ to the point $(0,3),$ as shown above?
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $3$ centered at $O.$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+9{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{9({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=9-{x}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =9-(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =9-9{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =9{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}9{sin}^{2}⁡t\cdot 3\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =27{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

Which of the following gives the line integral of the function f(x,y)=9−x2 along a circle of radius 3, traversed from the point (3,0) to the point (0,3), as shown above?

a
9∫0π/2cos2⁡tdt
b
27∫π/2πcos2⁡tdt
c
9∫0π/2sin2⁡tdt
d
27∫π/2πsin2⁡tdt
e
27∫0π/2sin2⁡tdt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫abf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt.

The curve C is a part-circle of radius 3 centered at O. It can be parametrized as

r(t)=⟨3cos⁡t,3sin⁡t⟩,0≤t≤π2.

Computing r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖, we get the following:

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(3cos⁡t)i+ddt(3sin⁡t)j=−3sin⁡ti+3cos⁡tj‖r′(t)‖=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2=(−3sin⁡t)2+(3cos⁡t)2=9sin2⁡t+9cos2⁡t=9(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=3

Now, since f(x,y)=9−x2, we obtain

f(r(t))=9−(3cos⁡t)2=9−9cos2⁡t=9sin2⁡t.

Therefore, we can write the integral as

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫0π/2f(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt=∫0π/29sin2⁡t⋅3⋅dt=27∫0π/2sin2⁡tdt.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing the Line Integral of a Function Over a Part-Circle
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057418/assets/4403bd230338dee226429d3f8f3ac8eaede1152aff0b6b18bd2e7ad9f3a3b8e3.png)

Which of the following gives the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=9-{x}^{2}$ along a circle of radius $3,$ traversed from the point $(3,0)$ to the point $(0,3),$ as shown above?
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $3$ centered at $O.$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+9{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{9({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=9-{x}^{2}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =9-(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =9-9{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =9{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}9{sin}^{2}⁡t\cdot 3\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =27{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}{sin}^{2}⁡t\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The circle is symmetric under (x,y)→(-x,y), which preserves arc length but changes xy√(y²+1) to its negative. Contributions therefore cancel, so the line integral is 0.

after.name: Question 11
after.problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=xy\sqrt{{y}^{2}+1}$ along the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=9.$
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a circle of radius $3$ centered at $O.$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+9{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{9({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy\sqrt{{y}^{2}+1},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\sqrt{(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+1} \\  & =9\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }9\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\cdot 3\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =27{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=9{sin}^{2}⁡t+1,$ $\text{d}u=18\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}27{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{1}^{1}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(0) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Question 11
?

Evaluate the line integral of the function f(x,y)=xyy2+1 along the circle C with equation x2+y2=9.

a
 0
b
 33
c
 9
d
 3
e
 3
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫abf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt.

The curve C is a circle of radius 3 centered at O. It can be parametrized as

r(t)=⟨3cos⁡t,3sin⁡t⟩,0≤t≤2π.

Computing r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖, we get the following:

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(3cos⁡t)i+ddt(3sin⁡t)j=−3sin⁡ti+3cos⁡tj‖r′(t)‖=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2=(−3sin⁡t)2+(3cos⁡t)2=9sin2⁡t+9cos2⁡t=9(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=3

Now, since f(x,y)=xyy2+1, we obtain

f(r(t))=(3cos⁡t)(3sin⁡t)(3sin⁡t)2+1=9cos⁡tsin⁡t9sin2⁡t+1.

Therefore, we can write the integral as

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫02πf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt=∫02π9cos⁡tsin⁡t9sin2⁡t+1⋅3⋅dt=27∫02πcos⁡tsin⁡t9sin2⁡t+1dt.

We can solve this using the substitution u=9sin2⁡t+1, du=18sin⁡tcos⁡tdt as follows:

27∫02πcos⁡tsin⁡t9sin2⁡t+1dt=32∫11udu=32(0)=0

after.name: Question 12
after.problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2}$ along the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16.$
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a circle of radius $4$ centered at $O.$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+16{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{16({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}-(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =16{cos}^{2}⁡t-16{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =16({cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =16\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }16\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\cdot 4\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =64{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=2t,$ $\text{d}u=2\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}64{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t & =32{\int }_{0}^{4\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡u\,\text{d}u \\  & =32\operatorname{sin}⁡u{|}_{0}^{4\pi } \\  & =32(0-0) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

We will use the formula

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫abf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt.

The curve C is a circle of radius 4 centered at O. It can be parametrized as

r(t)=⟨4cos⁡t,4sin⁡t⟩,0≤t≤2π.

Computing r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖, we get the following:

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(4cos⁡t)i+ddt(4sin⁡t)j=−4sin⁡ti+4cos⁡tj‖r′(t)‖=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2=(−4sin⁡t)2+(4cos⁡t)2=16sin2⁡t+16cos2⁡t=16(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=4

Now, since f(x,y)=x2−y2, we obtain

f(r(t))=(4cos⁡t)2−(4sin⁡t)2=16cos2⁡t−16sin2⁡t=16(cos2⁡t−sin2⁡t)=16cos⁡(2t).

Therefore, we can write the integral as

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫02πf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt=∫02π16cos⁡(2t)⋅4⋅dt=64∫02πcos⁡(2t)dt.

We can solve this using the substitution u=2t, du=2dt as follows:

64∫02πcos⁡(2t)dt=32∫04πcos⁡udu=32sin⁡u|04π=32(0−0)=0

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms d. With r(t)=(4cos(t),4sin(t)), the speed is 4 and x²-y²=16cos(2t). Thus the integral is 64∫₀²πcos(2t)dt=32[sin(2t)]₀²π=0.

$$

$$

decision.explanation: Parametrize the arc by r(t)=(4cos(t),4sin(t)), 3π/2≤t≤2π, with speed 4. The integral is 16∫cos(t)e^{4sin(t)-3}dt. Substituting u=4sin(t)-3 gives 4∫₋₇⁻³e^u du=4(e⁻³-e⁻⁷)=(4e⁴-4)/e⁷, option d.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057418/assets/e27774d260c053a7835b30e62c2d4b41be4b8dc22efcba8f7aa95704590561cf.png)

Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y-3}$ along the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=16,$ traversed from the point $(0,-4)$ to the point $(4,0),$ as shown above.
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $4$ centered at $O.$ It can be parametrized as  

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{3\pi }{2}\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+16{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{16({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y-3},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{4\operatorname{sin}⁡t-3}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{4\operatorname{sin}⁡t-3}\cdot 4\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{4\operatorname{sin}⁡t-3}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=4\operatorname{sin}⁡t-3,$ $\text{d}u=4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}4{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{4\operatorname{sin}⁡t-3}\,\text{d}t & =4{\int }_{-7}^{-3}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =4\,{e}^{u}{|}_{-7}^{-3} \\  & =4({e}^{-3}-{e}^{-7}) \\  & =\frac{4}{{e}^{3}}-\frac{4}{{e}^{7}} \\  & =\frac{4{e}^{4}-4}{{e}^{7}}\end{aligned}
$$

Question 13
?

Evaluate the line integral of the function f(x,y)=xey−3 along the circle C with equation x2+y2=16, traversed from the point (0,−4) to the point (4,0), as shown above.

a
 1e7
b
 1−e4e7
c
 0
d
 4e4−4e7
e
 2+4e7e4
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫abf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt.

The curve C is a part-circle of radius 4 centered at O. It can be parametrized as

r(t)=⟨4cos⁡t,4sin⁡t⟩,3π2≤t≤2π.

Computing r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖, we get the following:

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(4cos⁡t)i+ddt(4sin⁡t)j=−4sin⁡ti+4cos⁡tj‖r′(t)‖=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2=(−4sin⁡t)2+(4cos⁡t)2=16sin2⁡t+16cos2⁡t=16(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=4

Now, since f(x,y)=xey−3, we obtain

f(r(t))=4cos⁡te4sin⁡t−3.

Therefore, we can write the integral as

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫3π/22πf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt=∫3π/22π4cos⁡te4sin⁡t−3⋅4⋅dt=4∫3π/22π4cos⁡te4sin⁡t−3dt.

We can solve this using the substitution u=4sin⁡t−3, du=4cos⁡tdt as follows:

4∫3π/22π4cos⁡te4sin⁡t−3dt=4∫−7−3eudu=4eu|−7−3=4(e−3−e−7)=4e3−4e7=4e4−4e7

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057418/assets/cbd92b205693f1056e4dc2d0fc8154843e62b433b66d9b0ba8918d7f5bb3b8bf.png)

Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}$ along the circle $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4,$ traversed from the point $(-2,0)$ to the point $(0,-2),$ as shown above.
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

The curve $C$ is a part-circle of radius $2$ centered at $O.$ It can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\pi \le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=x{e}^{y}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\cdot 2\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =2{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t,$ $\text{d}u=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}2{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,{e}^{2\operatorname{sin}⁡t}\,\text{d}t & =2{\int }_{0}^{-2}{e}^{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =2{e}^{u}{|}_{0}^{-2} \\  & =2{e}^{-2}-2{e}^{0} \\  & =\frac{2}{{e}^{2}}-2\end{aligned}
$$
